practice_items.atom_title: Unauthorized physical access (tailgating, piggybacking, lock bypass)
practice_items.prompt: An attacker carries boxes to appear busy and follows an employee through a badge-reader door without swiping. This is BEST described as:
practice_items.explain: Tailgating = following an authorized person through a secured entry without the authorized person's knowledge or consent. The employee did not knowingly allow entry.

practice_items.atom_title: Unauthorized physical access (tailgating, piggybacking, lock bypass)
practice_items.prompt: Which physical attack leaves evidence in a badge-access log that looks identical to a legitimate single entry?
practice_items.explain: Both tailgating and piggybacking produce only one badge-swipe event in the log even though two people passed through. Lock picking and bump keying bypass the reader entirely.

practice_items.atom_title: Unauthorized physical access (tailgating, piggybacking, lock bypass)
practice_items.prompt: Select ALL techniques that can grant physical access WITHOUT the correct badge credential.
practice_items.explain: Tailgating bypasses the reader socially; RFID cloning replays a copied credential; lock picking bypasses the lock mechanically. MFA is a defensive control, not an attack.

practice_items.atom_title: Unauthorized physical access (tailgating, piggybacking, lock bypass)
practice_items.prompt: A building access log shows badge ID 1042 swiping door D1 at 09:00:02 and door D2 (40 meters away) at 09:00:05. Why is this record suspicious?
practice_items.explain: Three seconds is insufficient to walk 40 meters; this suggests the badge was passed to a second person, a replay attack, or a log integrity issue.

practice_items.atom_title: Unauthorized physical access (tailgating, piggybacking, lock bypass)
practice_items.prompt: Older 125 kHz HID proximity cards are especially vulnerable to which attack?
practice_items.explain: 125 kHz proximity cards broadcast their ID without cryptographic protection; a hidden reader can capture and clone them in seconds.

practice_items.atom_title: Unauthorized physical access (tailgating, piggybacking, lock bypass)
practice_items.prompt: Name the physical security control that uses two interlocked doors to prevent a second person from following through a secured entry.
practice_items.explain: A mantrap (also called an airlock or sally port) keeps one door locked until the first closes, eliminating the physical opportunity for tailgating.

practice_items.prompt: Why do data centers use clean-agent fire suppression (e.g., FM-200, inert gas) instead of water sprinklers?
options: Water sprinklers would themselves destroy the electronics they are meant to protect
Clean-agent systems are cheaper to install
Clean-agent systems put out fires faster than water in all cases
Fire codes prohibit water sprinklers in any commercial building
practice_items.explain: Water-based sprinklers short-circuit and corrode electronics, so they would cause the same loss the fire threatens. Clean-agent systems suppress fire by removing oxygen or interrupting combustion without wetting equipment.

practice_items.prompt: A server room's temperature sensor and humidity sensor both cross their warning thresholds at the same time. What does this combined pattern most likely indicate?
options: A failing or overloaded HVAC (cooling) system
practice_items.explain: Rising temperature together with drifting humidity is the classic signature of an HVAC failure, since the same cooling system regulates both.

practice_items.prompt: Which TWO controls directly address power-related environmental risk? Select all that apply.
practice_items.explain: A UPS bridges short outages/dips, and a redundant generator covers longer outages. Fire suppression addresses fire risk; raised flooring addresses water/flood risk.

practice_items.prompt: Why is raised flooring used as a control against water/flood risk in a data center?
practice_items.explain: Raised flooring physically elevates equipment above the slab, so a shallow flood or leak does not immediately reach the hardware.

practice_items.prompt: Why should environmental risks (power, HVAC, fire, water) be analyzed with the same rigor as a targeted cyberattack?
options: They are legally required to be reported the same way
They can produce the same availability or integrity loss as a targeted attack, even without an adversary
They are actually more common than cyberattacks in every organization
practice_items.explain: The CIA triad does not care whether the cause was malicious; a power failure, fire, or flood can take systems offline or corrupt data just as effectively as an attacker would.

practice_items.prompt: What is the single most effective control against data exposure from a STOLEN laptop?
practice_items.explain: A login password only protects the normal OS boot path; an attacker with physical possession can often boot from external media and read the disk directly. Full-disk encryption makes the drive's contents unreadable without the key even if removed.

practice_items.prompt: What distinguishes an evil-maid attack from ordinary device theft?
options: The device is covertly tampered with and returned, so the owner does not know anything happened
It always involves a hotel employee specifically
It only targets mobile phones, not laptops
It requires no physical access at all
practice_items.explain: The defining feature of an evil-maid attack is that the attacker briefly accesses the device, tampers with it (e.g., a fake boot loader that captures the disk-encryption password), and restores its appearance, the owner has no idea the device was compromised.

practice_items.prompt: Which TWO of the following are physical/behavioral signs that a device tampering incident may have occurred? Select all that apply.
options: A tamper-evident seal shows a torn or VOID pattern
The device's login password was recently changed by the owner
An unfamiliar dongle is found plugged into the keyboard port
The device was rebooted after a routine software update
practice_items.explain: A broken tamper-evident seal is direct physical evidence of tampering, and an unfamiliar USB implant (like a keylogger dongle) is a classic hardware-tampering sign. A user-initiated password change or a routine update reboot are normal, expected activity.

practice_items.prompt: Why can a tampering incident still be a risk even if the tamper-evident seal is intact?
practice_items.explain: Some tampering, such as plugging in a rogue USB keylogger or malicious peripheral, does not require opening the device's enclosure at all, so an intact seal does not rule out tampering.

practice_items.prompt: A stolen laptop was encrypted, contained sensitive data, and was not reported missing for 60 hours. Per this atom's triage rules, what risk level should this incident receive?
practice_items.explain: Encrypted (not HIGH), but sensitive data plus more than 48 hours since the last check triggers the MEDIUM rule, the long detection delay raises risk even though the disk itself is protected.
